When he wasn't doing anything.

Well, I'd come back and... Just by the time I knew they were gonna close up, see. Well, I know the man ain't made no money. You know, I'm working regular. Yeah, man. Paying this much I made for the whole side. You know, the nice side. Mm-hmm. Well, that's how we used to get along. I had a little fella named George Washington. Nice trombone player. I sent him in here for a moment. Laughhead, do's at him. Him and his wife. He was out there with more rain in. They wasn't doing nothing. Wasn't makin' no money. I said, man. I was playing with Eve Ann Thomas. Black Eagle Band. I said, man, you wanna go in home?
I said, man.

I said, man. I said, man. I said, man. I can't get any out of this fella's thick. I said, man. I can't get any out of this fella's thick. I said, you ain't doing nothing out of here, man. You're sleeping in the station here waiting for Ma Rainey to... get some tickets from Baton Rouge or somewhere to pull you all in there. And then two chairs in one. She's gonna take all the money. She's gonna take all the money. Still ain't gonna have nothing.

And I, the man was in the place, Cameron. I called him on the side, I said, man, I get about $75. What you gonna do with the money? I said, well, one of my good friends right there stranded. I'm gonna send him home. Who is that friend? When he come over the station, he didn't know George Washington. Little bit of fella played trombone. Good trombone player. I introduced him to Ma Rainey and George Washington and the whole cast sitting up there waiting for a telegram. Come from Baton Rouge somewhere to pull him into Baton Rouge. I wasn't gonna tell them that, you know. And I said George, $50. Well, his grandmother, his aunt was living down Thaddeus Street then. He said, well, I guess the next thing's smoking. All of them sitting up there asleep. He got out from there. Come on in the order. Mm-hmm. Poor little fella died. He was waking a long time, probably in the canal up there. Remember in, uh, Sonny Henry? That was J.J. dance too. Sidney Correa. All work up there. When I left here, that's where he was waking.
But when did he die?
Well, when he died, he stayed on Washington near Jackson. On Washington near Jackson?
Yeah, George Washington.

George Washington. One of these times. Now he, he and Louis Armstrong come up together back there in the Joneses home. He could play a baritone, bass on, and trombone. Mm-hmm. And he was good. See, I don't see nothing in that book. You know, I'll show you that book I have. No. I got a book of, you know, old musicians.
Which book is it? What color is it?

I thought I should see. What color is it? I got two, man. I got, with a yellow back on it. Then I got another book. Right there. Oh man, I thought that you should. I'll bring you now, Sonny. You gonna be there, Sonny?
Yeah, I'll be there, Sonny.
Yeah. Tim was told me he was gonna have a parade. I'll bring them books here. I'll show you, Sonny.
We might have them here, I just wanted the names of them.
Got all the old musicians.
And I've seen a picture of George Washington with Buddy.
Yeah, Buddy and Faisal.
Yeah, and Buddy Manatee.
Buddy Manatee bandit player.
And let's see, who else is in the band? Chester's out there. Chester and Edmund Hall, I think that's the band. And they had Earl Foster singing with them in the picture.
Over in Mandeville. Mandeville, yeah. Well, that's where they was. They were bootlegged for back over there. Oh, yeah.
He stayed there.

He made a good reputation over there. After he... I had Buddy message bandit the same as Chris did. Chris had a line of work around him, man. He was working, exactly, every night. Five nights every week, sometimes, every night. They take them double dates. Mm-hmm. All right, now.
You hire him.

Play up your own Pine Street, you know. Mm-hmm. He take that date. He take a date. Mm-hmm. I tell you, the old one talk, he used to run out there every Friday night. Mm-hmm. That lady used to run that talk out there. Another lady, we have a coffee now. But he had all that. But now, what he do? He take them dates. Sometimes, he have three dates. Why he break his band up? Why he go on one date? Can't you tell him? I tell him, the old one talk, he used to run out there every Friday night. Mm-hmm. That lady used to run that talk out there. And another lady, we have a coffee now. Why he had all that? But now, what he do? He take them dates. Sometimes, he have three dates. Why he break his band up? Why he go on one date? Why he go on one date? I tell some people. You know, when you hire Chris Kelly's band, you want to see the band. You don't want to see Chris Kelly and see surroundings with somebody else. with somebody else, you know. Even if they can't play, it's good. Guess he'd get them amateurs, you know. He'd blow. That wasn't coming up, you know. People knew him and knew the band. He's there, all right. Now, he sent us someplace else. He sent another trumpet player. Probably be just as good as he was. But that wasn't Chris Kelly. I said, he lost his way. I'm telling you, I'm the truth. He had this town sewed up for a long time. In town, Mobile, Montgomery, Barman Air, you know, these fellas up there, you know, help us. Tulane University. Remember, he's come back here. Right back in this section, he had somebody. He used to have them. Well, what these fellas do up there, they change bands. You know, they have Five Lines, Dixie Land band. Probably have Buddy Petit's band. The next side of the night, Chris Kelly. You know, just rode around like that. Every side of the night, they dance up there. But, that's where the fellas mixed up. They're looking for Bob Lyons band. Bob Lyons will come up there with a different band. Well, you don't want that. You don't hide Bob Lyons band. That's how they mixed up.
Yeah.
That's how Chris died. Bob Lyons band. As far as playing, boy, he could play. When that band got together, they had a pretty good band. Dixie Land band.
What did Mealy Barnes play like then, in those days?
Listen, man, Mealy, Mealy Barnes is, during, I haven't heard him play in over 25 years. But that, you hear how Willie played?
Mm-hmm.
Mealy didn't play, you know, as loud as Willie. You know what I mean? But he had the execution on the clarinet. These fellas playing something like it.
Mm-hmm.
Mealy Barnes used to be one of the best clarinet players around.
Who would you say was the best of all the clarinet around here? I'm talking about, not for reading, but for,
for a real tough reason. Dixieland.
Dixieland, you know.
Well, I, I haven't heard more.
But I mean, when you were here, when you were living here before you moved back.

Yeah, see, well, Bill used to play saxophone and, you know, alternate. But since he's been playing clarinet, he's slowing up a little bit. But now, Ed Dutre plays a whole lot of clarinet, you know. Sam Dutre. Which one?
You know, the son plays here now.
Yeah, well, that's the only one.
Yeah, you're talking about him now. He plays good. Yeah, he plays well. Oh, yeah.
I think it'd be a kind of, I'm talking water between him and Bill. Yeah.
What about, what about in the 20s and before that, 1910s, 1920s, who was good then?
China plays? Mm-hmm. Dixon and. Mm-hmm. Well,
not necessarily the one you'd pick as the best,
but you can name several,
you know.
Johnny Dotson, yeah, didn't he?
Yeah. You rated him high, huh? Yeah,
Johnny Dotson. Mm-hmm. And, uh, next ball house man, uh, mm-hmm. George Floyd, good. Yeah. You, you never met George Floyd?
No,

I never met him. You saw his picture? Pontius told me a lot about him. George Floyd. he, he, he was, good in my lip lady. Wanted to plant it now. And then another. Boyd come in there, now, son Henry used to play a whole lot of clank, huh? Mm-hmm. Johnny Henry.
Mm-hmm.
He started playing saxophone, he wouldn't pick up a clank. That guy played a whole lot of clank.
Yeah, it's funny, he can't play clarinet anymore, much.
Couldn't talk to him, into it, after he picked up that saxophone.
Mm-hmm. No.
No. I had a fella named, um, I don't know if he called him, guy, his name was Robichaud. He was a soft kind of player, but he could, he could play.
Who did he play with? Jack Carey. Yeah. Why don't you tell me about him too? Yeah. Robichaud. Yeah, he was good, huh?
Yeah, he was here for a reserve somewhere up there. He died up there.
I wanted to ask you about this guy that played banjo.
Oh, yeah. Guy got somebody killing me on Rambo Street there.
Well, I heard about that.

Yeah, guy was good. One of the best bands you played around in. Great big brother, strapping brother. Played trombone, too. That's what I wanted to ask you about. Yeah, he played trombone in the Armwood Band with me.
I never did understand how he could just double like that and not have any trouble, huh?
Well, he was a musical in kind.
Yeah, he was good enough to play in the Armwood Band and he played banjo regular.

Yeah, he played banjo. He played with Sam Morgan, man. He meet, halfway meet, you know, Sam Morgan come out. Sam Morgan at one time had a tough band on him. Different kind of music altogether, but... People like it.
What kind of music did he have, Sam?

Soft. Nothing boisterous. Tempo is big. And guys are together. We had Yank Johnson. On trombone. Good trombone, brother. Joe Watson on clarinet. Guy on paranger. Eddie. Get his name now. Next time I seen him playing bass on him. On Alexander, Virginia. Little Eddie. Little Eddie. Good bass violin player. Did he have a nickname? No, I always call him Eddie. And Alfred was playing drums.
Alfred Williams.

Alfred, Steady Temple. He had a tempo man there. Well, when them guys pull up on the corner, they wouldn't buck. You know what I mean? Sam Morgan never bucked. Ain't nobody. But wherever they played, the people would follow him.
I wonder about that place player. His name was Eddie, huh? What other bands did he play with? Yeah.
Nah. First time I saw him, he played with the Liberty Bell Band. That's been a long time ago.
Well, was he a...
Eddie Gilmore. His name is Gilmore. Eddie Gilmore.
T-Boy.
Yeah.
T-Boy, that's who I thought you were talking about.
Yeah.
T-Boy Gilmore. Because he and Dad were great buddies.
Yeah. Little short dad.
Yeah.
Yeah, I talked to one of Dad's little cousin there. Vincent. Mm-hmm. Yeah, he's a great guy.
Yeah, well, you know, he used to live right down the corner. Cater's in Liberty. When he died. With the Ogdens.
Well, that's where his people stay there. I seen a little fella there yesterday. Mm-hmm. I got home. Mm-hmm. He got there. Looked like it's all in their family.
Yeah, I think so.
Yeah. Little Dad. Mm-hmm. He was in our band. Yeah. Dad. Couldn't hear. Talk. Talk loud to him. Mm-hmm. But that music. Was in his ears.
Mm-hmm.
Couldn't make a bad note.
No.

He'd tell you. He'd tell you wouldn't make a bad note. He was in his ears. He was hard to hear. Mm-hmm. But the music looked like this run into his ears. Mm-hmm. He couldn't make a bad note. He didn't tell you. He was in his ears. He was in his ears. He was in his ears. He was in his ears. Now he was hard of hearing to talk to, but the music looked like this running into his ears. He couldn't make no bad note any time.

He'd get up and tell you. You split a note. Ah, man. That note didn't sound so good, huh? It sound good to you out there, huh? The note didn't sound so good. You split a note there, you know. Yeah. One of the fellas, he had another, he had two brothers. One of them played bass violin. The other fella, he couldn't play too much mandolin, but he carried the mandolin. And they used to match together on carnival day. You couldn't hire him. I'm the only one who hired him on carnival day. You know what? Because him and his three brothers mashed together. Babies and everything like that was him. The biggest one, he played bass violin. He was a magnolia. Dad used to say at that time, a magnolia and a million. Good days. I was going to get Dad and say, no, man, that don't count.
Listen, I wanted to ask you a few things. You know, just, when were you born and where and that kind of stuff? That's okay. Yeah, when were you born exactly?
1902, September the 9th. And where were you born? New Orleans, Louisiana. Jenna and Robinson.
Near where Percy's home is now.
That's right, right at the corner. See where that parking lot is?
Mm-hmm.
That's where it's born.
And I wanted you to tell me more about your, the way you grew up. Did you hear much music around the house when you were growing up?
Oh, yeah. Sure. See, after my mother died, went to Aime, Louisiana, and stayed there until, I think about, I was six years old, I think, when my mother died.
Mm-hmm.
My sister was baby. My sister was about four. I must have been sick. Bill must have been about eight. It's, you know, it's about two years apart.
Mm-hmm.

When they Aime of Louisiana and stayed out there and went to school out there, you're in the country there. They give you three months school and when the crop come in, you turn out to school to pick up the crop. Mm-hmm. All like that. Well, after then, I got about 10, 12 years old. My father, he's going to California, I think. Well, my head come up there and got us, got me in prison for us in the island. Stayed right out there. You just, see where you just left out there?
Mm-hmm. That long house?
Well, that's where we stayed. Absolutely.
Which long house? Right behind, you see where I hang them clothes at? Mm-hmm. Right there.
Yeah. That's where we lived at. Mm-hmm. My aunt practically took care of us. Mm-hmm. And my grandfather was a musician, you know, a music teacher.
Mm-hmm.
Came up there. Everybody in that house had to learn something about music. Mm-hmm. Well, I picked out, first I picked out a guitar, he said, no. Anything else, he had all kind of instruments.
Mm-hmm.

I think he got an old boy around there now, Bill, my neighbor. Pickle those flutes and everything. Well, look in the other corner and say, well, a shell is sitting over there. Well, I started on the page, you know, a shell. I grew the shell, and started on base power. stuff like stuff

of Earl Humphrey, Moetze 28th 1963. I'd just like to have it on the tape. In case we get the box mixed up. You were telling me about the bass. You took up the bass huh? Yeah. You couldn't make money huh?

No, well I didn't. Family bass. We had the rehearsal every Friday. There wasn't nobody but me and Bill, my granddaddy and my aunt. Because he taught, you know, his teachings. Neighborhood children come down there like T.V. Thomas, Eric Williams, and that big, big town at the, when out of California was healthy and died out there. In our front room there, we had to have about an hour in the air for a whistle every Friday night. And the people on the front, all that neighborhood up around there, wide end colored, come here to us play. And then here come, I start to play the trombone. Took a few lessons on the trombone. Got through noises. In the house, go out in the back and practice on that trombone. Mm-hmm. In the yard, the people got tired of hearing that noise out there. Mm-hmm. But I was in and out the house, practicing on that trombone. And then, what's the thing? Well, Well, Orr, I used to follow Orr, Kid Oliver, visiting at them place. Orr and who? Kid Oliver and Orr, they had a band together. Oh yeah. I'd go every Sunday night and miss me. Kid Oliver and Orr and Astor. Uh, God done touching on the horn and learning. I learned the horn and study. I had to study my music. When an old man called you in there for your lesson, now you better know that.
Mm-hmm.

After I started on trombone. That fella named Portris Market Dan, a guitar player. Mm-hmm. First job I went on. He played guitar. Went out Spanish for the West End or somewhere else. Played that job. Next son, he had another job. I went out there and trade. Well, I'm getting a little better and better all the time, see. Well, Those, uh, pavilions used to be, you know, just jammed up, you know, just about, say about 20 feet apart. Mm-hmm. Out there, you know.
Old time, long time, of course. Mm-hmm.

Manny, uh, Manny Gabriel. He heard me play. He had a weekend, you know, weekend job. Even him. Oh, good, wow. He's pretty nice trumpet player. Him and Duke Gabriel and his son played drums. Little Manny. What did Gabriel play now? The guitar. You know Gabriel played guitar.
I, uh, haven't met him.
Yeah, man. What, uh, you met?
Uh, Clarence Gabriel?
Yeah.
I never have met him, I don't think.
Yeah, Clarence. I know his brother, Percy. He's a little better fella.
I know Percy, the one that played the bass, but he's awful young. I doubt if you knew him. What did you know him?
Well, uh, August married one of, uh, uh, uh, uh, Miss Gabriel's daughter. You know August, the bass player?
Oh, Lanois. Oh, yeah.
The bass player.
Yeah, August Lanois.
Yeah, August Lanois. Well, he married, uh, one of, uh, I don't know. Yeah, he had, had, had two dollars, I know.
I hate to change the subject, but I want to know about this Portrait's Market Dan. Who did he bum with? If we could find anything about him.

Oh, yeah, man. He, Portrait's Market Dan, stayed in the district back then. And he, he guitar player. He couldn't sing, but he could talk and rhyme. He, he's a fool out there and, you know, them prostitutes all back in the district down there, you know, all around good time places. Him and George Jones and Cornelius and all them, that string aggregation. Well, when they needed some instruments, you know, blowing instruments, well, they come out and get them out there on the lake there, but they need some horns, you know, out there on the lake, because the wind will take that string music right on out.
But you don't know anybody who'd know where to find him or anything, huh? Oh, I expect a fella then, man.

Longer than that been, man. He's older than you, huh? Oh, yeah, he's an old fella then. Had kind of bad eye, Portrait's Market Dan. He stayed on Padida, and I, I'll tell you what kind of fella he was, where he lived at, you know. He stayed on Padida, on, on, lived it, between Padida and Portrait's, right in the heart of the district. At that time, it was rough, you know what I mean, the rough part of the district. No joke. Well, that's where he lived.
Well, I'll ask somebody who lived in that neighborhood.

We didn't call them Portrait's Market Dan, because he'd go around there and help on Portrait's and Rampart's, used to be a public market, it was up at 12 o'clock. He'd go around there and help them butchers, you know, scrape them stands off, and give them a whole lot of meat, you know. You know, meat they didn't think they were going to sell the next day, they'd be going to put in an ice box, they didn't have no refrigerators, they didn't put a hundred pound ice in an ice box, you know, keep that name. Well, he carried that stuff back then, he'd give to them prostitutes, you know,
a great big bag of stuff, a basket of stuff.

Gives to them people, they'd stir it up, you know, and get a meal off it. Well, that's called them Portrait's Market Dan. He'd help out a whole lot of people. And he'd go down and scrape that stand for them butchers, and they'd give them leftover meat, you know, all's in there. They'd put it in a box or something like that, and he'd get back then and give them people, underprivileged people. And he stayed in a little... Oh man, half of this would be... his two rooms. Mm-hmm. And stool and then his bed, you know, bastard-like. Yeah. But he had connection with some good people that would give him jobs. And then he'd add now... Willie Phillips with his trumpet pair. Mm-hmm. You heard about Willie Phillips. Oh yeah. With trumpet. Mm-hmm.
Who else would he hire? Cook Chapson.
You heard about Cook Chapson?
Yeah, his mama had a cook shop right around in there, didn't she?
I don't know, but...
Yeah, well, I heard Fats Bonetta talk about him.

Yeah. Good Chapson played the drum. Mm-hmm. And, uh, Willie... Willie Phillips, Dan... And... Used to hire another fella named Ike, one-leg Ike, played baseballin'. Last time I saw him, he got us in Texas. Ike Williams. That's the name, Ike Williams.
I heard, wasn't Ike Williams who played clarinet?
Yeah. He's talking clarinet.
Same guy?
No, no, no, this fella was older than that Ike Williams. This guy was an old fella, just same... About the same age that, uh, Rogers Market Dan was. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
And one, he had a pig-leg.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
He used to play, uh, bass. Mm-hmm. And then... After then... After then... When he couldn't get Ike, he got our bad Glennie.
Oh, yeah.
Anyway, he's a good baseball.

I knew him, yeah. I knew him. He was funny. He's a man who used to drink his whiskey, uh, drink his water first, and then he'd drink his whiskey to get that awful taste out of his mouth. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, we had fun, man. Yeah. We and Albert Glennie and T-boy.
Mm-hmm.
Nice.
I had Rayman T-boy Rayman. You ever meet him?
I never have met him. He comes back once in a while, but I never have met him.
Aye, we had a band. A Columbia band. In California, Bill said.
I never did know much about T-boy other than him being in the Eureka. You had a band with him. When was that?

Let's see now. That must have been band. Well, I'll play with T-boy and him. I'll come here. 1922. 23. At 24. T-boy. Eddie Dawson. You remember you met him? Oh yeah, I know him. I see him all the time.
You know, he's still working for the bank. Yeah, well that's...
Eddie Dawson. He been there over 20 years. About 40 years now.
And...
And... And... And...
And...
And... And... And... And... And... And... And...
Bill, I did ask about him.
About who? The drummer. About... About... About... About... About... great with country of them.
You don't know what band he was with regular?
Yeah, he did peer on all them fellas, ain't he?
He was as good as say Walter Brundy or Red Happy or those guys?
Well, I could estimate him over. Over them? Well, not over Walter Brundy.
Yeah, but over Red Happy.
Yeah, because on the reading ability. That's a boy named that. He played violin nice. He played nice drum.
That beats the hell out of me. I can't think of anybody who played violin and drums.

I can't think of that a while. Anyhow, he was secretary when they first set the union up there. He was secretary for the union. Celestine was the president. His name's Joe. I knew his name, his first name was Joe.
The drummer?
Yeah.
Did he play the slide whistle too? No.
You know one of them both whistles? No.
Not Joe Strutter.
Oh no, I know Joe Strutter.
Yeah. Uh, was this uh, I know Joe Lindsey played drums, but it couldn't be him.
No, not Joe Lindsey. I know Joe Lindsey. The only other drummer I can think of is Windy Joe Wynn.
You know Joe Wynn, but that's not him.
Yeah, well he's been going with me. He went to Penn School and kept on going. He broke up, he tried to break up the union. Joe Wynn.
Where did this drummer live?
Way down town. Paulette Lane.
Hmm.
Uh, Joe Welsh.
Oh yeah.
Joe Welsh.
Alright, I'll hurry him.

See like Alfred played? Uh huh. Same type of drummer. Steady, huh? Steady drummer. Then he could play a nice violin. His father was a musician. Could draw notes man. Looked like he'd come out to print. Uh huh. Mr. Welch. Was he a trumpet player, was it that one? was it that one? I can't remember. I don't know what Joe Welson's father played, because I know he used to play with my grandfather, but I never seen him. I met his mother and his sisters, and I know when they first set the union up here, he was secretary. Salas was voted for the president. And we had good bands. T-Boy always was a good guitar player. That's Ramey, T-Boy Ramey Adams. He was playing guitar, huh?
Yeah, he was one of the best around here. I only knew him as a trumpet player. He used to take him trumpet after. Who was your trumpet player in your band?

Well, T-Boy. Oh, when you had your band. Yeah, well I was playing with that line up, see? Joe Welsh, Eddie Dawson, Abbe Kearney, T-Boy, a little fellow named Arthur Williams, and Kearney. That kind of bad eye. I didn't see his name in that book. He was pretty good, too. Arthur Williams.
It's about five minutes or three. We better turn it off and get everything signed up and on. Yeah. Get paid up and all that. stuff

segments.title: Opening and introductions, Tulane Seminar Room
segments.summary: Allen identifies himself, the date and the location, and sets up to play a record.

segments.chapter: Ann Cook session and Buddy Petit stories
segments.title: Making the 1927 Ann Cook record, with Louis Dumaine
segments.summary: Humphrey hears the Ann Cook record, recalls making it after six weeks without playing, with no rehearsal, and how Louis coached her phrasing.

segments.chapter: Ann Cook session and Buddy Petit stories
segments.title: Red Onion Drag and the old house of detention district
segments.summary: Humphrey explains the Red Onion Drag name came from a red house behind the house of detention near James Alley, and recalls advertising wagons there.

segments.chapter: Ann Cook session and Buddy Petit stories
segments.title: Rip Them Up Joe and Buddy Petit making up tunes
segments.summary: Brief talk of who named 'Rip Them Up Joe' and Buddy Petit composing tunes as he went.

segments.chapter: Ann Cook session and Buddy Petit stories
segments.title: Playing summers at the Mandeville hotel with Lee Collins
segments.summary: Humphrey and Lee Collins held a Saturday-night summer contract at a Mandeville hotel; the men discuss the bass player and the Fritz brothers.

segments.chapter: Ann Cook session and Buddy Petit stories
segments.title: Baseball park gig and the train trip with Buddy Petit
segments.summary: Humphrey tells of playing for a colored baseball park, then the train ride with Buddy Petit, who stopped over and met Baptiste.

segments.title: Bucking contests from the advertising truck
segments.summary: Playing from a truck to advertise a baseball game, Humphrey describes bucking rival bands with Lee Collins and Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Playing with Johnny Brown's band and Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls working with Johnny Brown's band, Chris Kelly and Mealy Barnes, and the pressure rival players put on Kelly.

segments.title: How Chris Kelly won bucking contests with his plunger mute
segments.summary: Humphrey describes Chris Kelly's blues playing, his rubber mute, Leroy Evans' timekeeping and the numbers Kelly played.

segments.title: Garbled passage on the tape
segments.summary: A stretch of unintelligible repeated ASR text with a stray remark about Jim.

segments.title: Identifying Lee Collins on a record
segments.summary: Allen plays a record; Humphrey identifies Lee Collins ('Shags') and mentions Robert Thomas.

segments.title: Kelly's Careless Love and how Chris Kelly's band handled keys
segments.summary: Humphrey explains Chris Kelly's practice of calling keys, fade-outs, dancing rhythm and modulation compared to reading music.

segments.title: Reel two begins and a record by Lee Collins and Joe Robichaux
segments.summary: Allen marks reel two and plays records; Humphrey recalls jitney dance playing that went on all night for two years.

segments.title: Sonny Handy and the Astoria band with Rene Hall
segments.summary: Humphrey names the band of Roy Evans, Sonny Handy, Lee Collins, Joe Robichaux and Rene Hall, nicknamed Plectum for his five-string guitar.

segments.title: Rene Hall's long-necked plectrum banjo
segments.summary: The men discuss how Rene Hall played the five-string instrument, with a pick, and how he surprised the band with it.

segments.title: Moving to the Astoria and the Sunday jitney dance
segments.summary: Humphrey describes the Astoria job, pay of about $78, and the suburban jitney dance at La Vida.

segments.title: How the ticket-based taxi dance worked
segments.summary: Humphrey explains the dance-hall ticket system, dime dances and how the girls were paid, and the two-year job.

segments.title: First union in New Orleans and sitting in around the district
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls the arrival of the union, casual sitting-in before it, and sending trombonist George Washington to Ma Rainey's cast.

segments.title: Sending George Washington home from the Ma Rainey troupe
segments.summary: Humphrey recounts helping trombonist George Washington leave Ma Rainey's stranded show and his later death; Washington came up with Louis Armstrong.

segments.title: Humphrey's books of old musicians
segments.summary: Humphrey mentions two books of old musicians he will bring for Allen.

segments.title: Photo of George Washington with Buddy Manetta and others
segments.summary: Allen recalls a photo of George Washington, Buddy Manetta and others; Humphrey ties it to Mandeville.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's double-booking and the decline of his band
segments.summary: Humphrey criticizes Chris Kelly for sending substitutes to dates and how other bands competed for his work.

segments.title: Mealy Barnes and the best clarinetists in New Orleans
segments.summary: Humphrey rates Mealy Barnes, Willie and Ed and Sam Dutre as clarinet players.

segments.title: Clarinetists of the 1920s: Johnny Dotson, George Floyd, Johnny Handy
segments.summary: Allen asks who was good around 1920; Humphrey names Dotson, George Floyd, Sonny Henry and Robichaud.

segments.title: The banjoist-trombonist and Sam Morgan's band
segments.summary: Humphrey talks of a banjo player who also played trombone and of Sam Morgan's quiet, steady band and its members.

segments.title: Eddie Gilmore, bass player, and T-Boy
segments.summary: The men sort out the bass player's name as Eddie Gilmore, and Allen links it to T-Boy Gilmore and his own father.

segments.title: Little Dad, the hard-of-hearing musician in Humphrey's band
segments.summary: Humphrey remembers Little Dad, who was hard to talk to but never made a bad note, and his carnival-day brothers.

segments.title: Birth in 1902 and the family home
segments.summary: Humphrey gives his birth date, September 9, 1902, and place in New Orleans.

segments.title: Childhood after his mother's death, country school and return to town
segments.summary: After his mother died Humphrey lived in the country, attended short school terms, and later returned to the New Orleans house.

segments.title: Grandfather's music lessons, learning bass and trombone
segments.summary: Humphrey's grandfather taught music in the house; he started on bass, then trombone, and followed Kid Ory and Kid Oliver.

segments.title: First trombone jobs and the Gabriel family
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls his first jobs, Manny Gabriel hiring him, and the Gabriel family connections.

segments.title: Poydras Market Dan, the guitar player of the district
segments.summary: Humphrey describes Poydras Market Dan, guitarist who lived in the district and fed the poor with butcher stand scraps.

segments.title: Willie Phillips, Cook Chapson and Ike Williams
segments.summary: The men discuss musicians Market Dan hired, including Cook Chapson and Ike Williams, and the bass player with a peg leg.

segments.title: Playing with T-Boy and Eddie Dawson in the early 1920s
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls a band with T-Boy Remy and Eddie Dawson around 1922-24.

segments.title: Comparing a drummer with Walter Brundy and Red Happy
segments.summary: Allen and Humphrey rate an unnamed drummer-violinist against Walter Brundy and Red Happy.

segments.title: Early union officers and the drummer Joe Welsh
segments.summary: They try to identify the union secretary-drummer, settling on Joe Welsh, and Humphrey recalls the first union president.

segments.title: Lineup of Humphrey's band with T-Boy on trumpet
segments.summary: Humphrey names band members including Joe Welsh, Eddie Dawson, T-Boy and Arthur Williams.

segments.title: Closing the session
segments.summary: Allen ends the tape.
